topic: DP-3T: The Privacy-First Way to Trace Contacts
target_audience: University Students (Computer Science or Data Privacy)

outline.topic: DP-3T: The Privacy-First Way to Trace Contacts
outline.target_audience: University Students (Computer Science or Data Privacy)

sections.title: The Privacy Dilemma
sections.content: Introduce the challenge of contact tracing during a pandemic: How can we notify people exposed to a virus without creating a 'Big Brother' surveillance state that tracks everyone's identity and location?
sections.example: Characters: Alice and Bob. Alice meets Bob at a park. They want to be notified if the other gets sick later, but they don't want a central server to know they were at the park or who they are.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Cryptographic Hash Functions
sections.content: Explain the concept of a 'One-Way Hash Function'. A function H(x) that turns an input into a fixed-size 'fingerprint'. It is impossible to reverse, and even a tiny change in input results in a completely different output.
sections.example: Visual: A 'Digital Meat Grinder'. Put in a secret word (Input), get out a specific pattern of sausage (Hash). You can't turn the sausage back into the word.

sections.title: Step 1: Generating Daily Secrets and Ephemeral IDs
sections.content: Alice's phone generates a random Daily Secret Key (SK_t). Using a Hash function, the phone derives a series of 'Ephemeral IDs' (EphIDs) that change every 15 minutes. Math: EphID = PRF(SK_t, time_slot).
sections.example: Visual: A 'Secret Identity Factory'. Alice’s phone wears a different 'costume' (EphID) every 15 minutes. To an observer, these costumes look unrelated, but Alice's phone knows they all came from her Daily Secret.

sections.title: Step 2: The Bluetooth Handshake
sections.content: Devices use Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) to broadcast their current EphID and listen for others. If Alice and Bob are close, their phones exchange and store the EphIDs they hear, along with the date and signal strength (proximity), locally on the device.
sections.example: Visual: Alice's phone 'whispers' its current costume number to Bob's phone. Bob's phone writes it down in a private notebook and keeps it for 14 days.

sections.title: Step 3: Positive Diagnosis and Reporting
sections.content: If Alice tests positive, she voluntarily uploads her Daily Secret Keys (SKs) for the period she was infectious to a central server. Crucially, she does NOT upload her contacts or her location.
sections.example: Visual: Alice sends a list of her 'Daily Seeds' to a public bulletin board (the Server). The server doesn't know who she met; it only sees the seeds.

sections.title: Step 4: Local Matching and Notification
sections.content: Bob's phone periodically downloads the new 'Positive Secret Keys' from the server. His phone reconstructs all possible EphIDs from those keys and compares them against the list of IDs stored in his local notebook.
sections.example: Visual: Bob's phone takes Alice's Seed, runs the 'Identity Factory' to see all the costumes Alice wore, and realizes, 'Hey! I saw costume #842 on Tuesday!' Bob gets a private notification to get tested.

sections.title: Summary: Why it's Secure
sections.content: Review the decentralized nature of DP-3T. The server never sees the contact graph. Matching happens only on the user's device. No GPS or personal data is ever transmitted.
sections.example: Graphic: A comparison table. Centralized (Server knows all) vs. DP-3T (Server is a blind postman). Total time: 5:00.

storyboard.title: The Privacy Dilemma
lecture_lines: Contact tracing stops pandemics by identifying exposure risks.
But central tracking creates a "Big Brother" surveillance state.
How can we notify users while protecting their identity?
animations: Alice and Bob icons appear in a green park area (#2ECC71). A connection line pulses between them labeled 'Exposure Risk' (#E74C3C).

A large 'Central Server' icon (#95A5A6) appears at the top. Dotted lines from Alice, Bob, and many other dots connect to it, while a 'Big Brother' eye icon [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/eye.svg] overlays the server.

The eye icon [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/eye.svg] is crossed out with a red 'X' (#E74C3C). A question mark icon (#F1C40F) appears between Alice's phone [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/phone.svg] and a generic 'Notification' icon, emphasizing privacy.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: Cryptographic Hash Functions
lecture_lines: A hash function creates a unique digital fingerprint.
It is a one-way process, impossible to reverse.
Tiny input changes produce completely different results.
animations: An input box labeled 'Input Data' (#3498DB) moves into a 'Hash Function' box. A unique, complex hex string fingerprint (#ECF0F1) comes out.
Show the hex string fingerprint attempting to move back into the hash function box, but being blocked by a 'One-Way' barrier icon (#E74C3C).
Change 'Input Data' to 'Input Datb' (red 'b'). The resulting hex string fingerprint is shown next to the first one, completely different and highlighted in #F1C40F.

storyboard.title: Step 1: Generating Daily Secrets and Ephemeral IDs
lecture_lines: Alice's phone generates a random Daily Secret Key.
This key creates changing Ephemeral IDs every fifteen minutes.
To others, these IDs look like random, unrelated strings.
Only Alice’s phone knows the secret behind these IDs.
This rotation prevents tracking Alice's movements over time.
animations: Alice's phone [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/phone.svg] icon is shown. Inside, a glowing key labeled 'SK_t' (#F1C40F) is generated.
The 'SK_t' key feeds into a transformation process. Out pop five different labels: 'EphID_1' through 'EphID_5' (#3498DB), arranged on a timeline.
The 'EphID' labels are shown to an external 'Observer' icon (#95A5A6). Question marks appear above the observer, indicating they cannot link the IDs.
A dashed line connects all 'EphID' labels back to Alice's 'SK_t' inside her phone [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/phone.svg], highlighting the private connection.

Alice's phone [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/phone.svg] moves across the screen. At each position, a different 'EphID' is displayed, showing how the rotation prevents a continuous tracking path.

storyboard.title: Step 2: The Bluetooth Handshake
lecture_lines: Nearby phones exchange Ephemeral IDs using Bluetooth.
Bob’s phone stores Alice's ID and signal strength locally.
This record stays on the device for fourteen days.
animations: Alice and Bob phone [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/phone.svg] icons are close. A blue Bluetooth wave icon (#3498DB) pulses between them. Alice's current 'EphID_A' moves to Bob's phone [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/phone.svg].
Bob's phone [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/phone.svg] opens a 'Local Log' table. 'EphID_A' and a signal strength bar (#2ECC71) are written into a row.

A calendar [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/calendar.svg] icon appears next to the log, showing a countdown from 14 to 0. At day 0, the log entry fades out to show local deletion.

storyboard.title: Step 3: Positive Diagnosis and Reporting
lecture_lines: If Alice tests positive, she voluntarily reports her keys.
She uploads her Daily Secret Keys to a server.
Crucially, no personal identities or locations are shared.
The server only sees a list of anonymous keys.
This protects Alice’s privacy while enabling notification.
animations: Alice's phone turns red (#E74C3C) with a 'Positive' icon. An 'Upload Keys?' confirmation prompt appears.
Alice's 'SK_t' keys for the last 14 days move from her phone to a central 'Diagnosis Server' (#95A5A6).
A 'Location' pin and 'Identity' ID-card icon appear on Alice's side but are blocked by a green shield (#2ECC71) from being uploaded.
On the server, a list of hex keys (#ECF0F1) is displayed with no names or locations attached.
A 'Notification' icon (#F1C40F) pulses on the server, signifying its role in informing others without tracking Alice.

storyboard.title: Step 4: Local Matching and Notification
lecture_lines: Bob’s phone downloads new positive keys from the server.
It reconstructs all Ephemeral IDs from those secret keys.
Bob's phone compares these against IDs in its notebook.
If a match is found, Bob is notified privately.
The matching process happens entirely on Bob’s device.
animations: Bob's phone downloads the list of 'Positive SKs' from the central server into its local storage.
Bob's phone uses the downloaded keys to generate a list of 'Reconstructed EphIDs' (#3498DB).
A comparison animation shows the 'Reconstructed EphIDs' being checked against Bob's 'Local Log'. One pair of IDs flashes green (#2ECC71) for a match.
Bob's phone displays a 'Possible Exposure' alert (#E74C3C) with instructions.
A border glows around Bob's phone, labeled 'Local Process' (#F1C40F), emphasizing the server is never informed of the match.

storyboard.title: Summary: Why it's Secure
lecture_lines: The server never sees the actual contact graph.
Matching is decentralized, occurring only on the user's phone.
DP-3T ensures safety without compromising individual privacy.
animations: A network of nodes and lines (contact graph) is shown. A server icon [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/server.svg] (#95A5A6) is shown with a 'No Entry' sign (#E74C3C) over the graph.
Two phone icons [Asset: /mmfs1/data/home/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/phone.svg] are shown with rotating gears (#F1C40F) inside them to represent decentralized matching logic.
A comparison table appears: 'Centralized' shows a red 'X' for privacy, while 'DP-3T' shows a green checkmark (#2ECC71). Title: 'Privacy through Decentralization'.
